the use of opioids in the treatment of musculoskeletal pain is associated with an increased likelihood of disability, an increased risk of overdose morbidity and/or mortality, and a greater chance of dependence and/or addiction.

the use of opioids is not recommended for treating chronic noncancer musculoskeletal pain.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
opioids should be prescribed only after nonpharmacological and nonopioid pharmacological therapies are considered and found to be ineffective.
opioids should only be used when there is a clear indication for the use of opioids and that the risks and benefits are clearly understood and discussed.
the opioid epidemic is not a result of a lack of education.
The main takeaway from our work is that
injured workers should be treated with non-opioid medications and therapies whenever possible.
injured workers with musculoskeletal disorders who have pain and who are prescribed opioids are more likely to be disabled and have higher costs than those who do not receive opioid prescriptions.
opioid prescribing should be done cautiously and only after careful consideration of all other treatment options, including nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic therapies.
